lessons.text: Remotion's HtmlInCanvasMotionBlur (4.0.529+, 8 samples by default, 180-degree shutter, no nesting, preview behind a Chrome flag) is worth testing against Slate's sub-frame renderer, which stays the default.

destination.reason: Deferred by the plan: Remotion stays pinned at 4.0.521 until a parity check (HtmlInCanvasMotionBlur needs 4.0.529 or later), and render_mb stays the default; engine/README.md records the test to run before any switch.

lessons.text: Tune render concurrency per machine with npx remotion benchmark instead of the default (half the CPU threads), which can overload the machine and crash renders.

destination.note: At most half the cores and never more than 8, with one render slot and the runner's load guard; no per-machine benchmark yet.

lessons.text: Remotion performance notes: prefer @remotion/media's Video over OffthreadVideo, precompute GPU-heavy CSS (blur, shadows, gradients) on GPU-less machines, and use PNG frames only where alpha or lossless averaging needs them.

terms: PNG frames are only for where alpha or lossless averaging needs them
Prefer the kit's own components to heavy CSS

lessons.text: Remotion ProRes: profiles run proxy to 4444-xq (hq by default); alpha needs 4444 plus PNG frames and yuva444p10le; crf is unsupported and videoBitrate ignored.

destination.reason: Slate never uses Remotion's own ProRes encoder: render_mb streams PNG sub-frames to ffmpeg's prores_ks (422 HQ), and no format asks for alpha.

lessons.text: Remotion's distributed renders need equal chunk frame ranges (except the last), identical options, h264-ts chunks, an enforced audio track, compositionStart and seamless AAC (or PCM) audio, merged with combineChunks().

destination.note: Slate chunks its own way, not with Remotion's distributed rendering: lossless chunks over exact frame ranges, no audio in chunks, joined by one encode with a PSNR scan at every join (render/joins.py).

lessons.text: HyperFrames (Apache-2.0: HTML and seekable animation to deterministic MP4) is prior art for the open web renderer; its router skill, frozen-file asset ledger and non-interactive skill updates are patterns to learn from.

destination.note: Slate's open web renderer is its own (a seekable local page, captured frame by frame), with HyperFrames noted as prior art in engine/web/README.md.

lessons.text: claude-motion-design (HTML plus Playwright plus ffmpeg, no Remotion licence) is prior art for a Remotion-free renderer; Slate's version captures only its own local pages with puppeteer and never browses.

destination.note: puppeteer loads only the renderer's own local page; any network request fails the render, so it never becomes a second browser.

lessons.text: Renders run locally, never on the WORK machine, one act at a time at the delivery bar, and a render replaces the registered file only when its frame count matches the registry span; otherwise the old render stays and the job reports failure.

destination.note: Gate render.act<N>.frames. The no-WORK rule is held by tests/render/test_render_no_work.py.

lessons.text: After every act render, stamp its registry entry and run the glitch scan, writing the flags beside the render.

destination.note: Every act render is stamped in renders/registry.json with its proof; `slate qa glitch` scans each registered render (cached by its hash), and the render command names that next step.

lessons.text: Renders run at a lower CPU priority so the machine stays usable for everything else.

Generate the render registry from shots.json (one entry per act with its span), keep an entry's history only when its range and file are unchanged, and assert acts cover 0 to the film's total frames; two films kept theirs by hand.

destination.note: The registry is written by `slate render` from timing/shots.json (one entry per act with its span); an entry whose act range moved reports as needing a render.

lessons.text: The fast-variant editor refuses tracks with a single key (it needs two or more), zero-width masks, and GLSL that paints outside its raster box.

terms: it refuses tracks with a single key

lessons.text: In the fast-variant editor, motion blur on frames whose children have shadows makes hard, fringed halos; skip blur on shadow-bearing frames.

terms: motion blur on frames whose children have shadows

lessons.text: The fast-variant editor rasterizes a node's mask at canvas size from the node's own origin (feathering softens that raster's edges), and mask width grows from the mask's centre.

terms: it rasterizes a node's mask at canvas size

lessons.text: The fast-variant editor's presigned upload slots expire in under an hour, despite a stated 24 hours; upload right before use.

terms: its upload slots expire in under an hour

lessons.text: The fast-variant editor's 16-sample motion-blur cap shows steps on whips; ramp the blur instead.

terms: its 16-sample blur cap shows steps on whips

lessons.text: The fast-variant editor's sandbox runs cost no credits and render about 67 ms a frame at 1080p, but a 100 s render took 94-577 s end to end.
The fast-variant editor's workflow docs live only behind the vendor's connector; record the version used with each variant.

terms: record the version used with every variant

lessons.text: The toolchain proof is a scripted After Effects smoke test: build a one-second comp with one shape on a brand ease, render it with aerender, require every frame, and measure the ease in pixels against the code curve (the film's entrance ease matched within 1.5 px from frame 6 on; the first motion-blurred frame measured 4.2 px). AE-applied eases must match the code eases.

destination.note: The limit is 1% of the move's travel on the worst frame.

also.note: The same ease vectors run in pytest, vitest and an ExtendScript runner (tests/ae/test_ae_kit.py::test_extendscript_runner_passes_the_shared_vectors).

lessons.text: After Effects' "Allow Scripts to Write Files and Access Network" is the owner's security choice: only they switch it, and if a reset turns it off, Slate says so and never turns it back on. The finishing route works with it off by reporting through AE's preferences file.

terms: security setting, and only they change it

also.note: Scripts report back through app.settings when the preference is off.

terms: Only the owner turns that on

lessons.text: The AE finish is a project built from data: one comp per shot holding its slice of the act render, one comp per act in order, and a master comp with the final mix and markers for every shot, spoken word and timeline event; the masters render there.

terms: markers per shot, word and event
destination.note: `slate ae build --go` (slate.ae.project.build) writes the spec from film.json and runs this.

terms: builds the project from data: one comp per shot showing its slice of the act render

lessons.text: Before any rebuild, save whatever AE project is open (to a preserved folder) and never discard user work; probes run only in an empty untitled project and clean up after themselves.

destination.note: Unsaved work is saved to the preserve folder before any fresh project replaces it (SL.freshProject); tests/ae/test_ae_project.py::test_build_preserves_unsaved_work.

terms: Open projects are preserved before any rebuild

lessons.text: Set the AE project's working space to the profile AE assigns to the incoming footage (Rec.709 Gamma 2.4 for BT.709-tagged renders) so AE converts nothing: an sRGB working space made a deep brand colour about 8 code values darker (33 dB) and BT.709-5 was worse, while the matching space stays under half a code value (50 to 53 dB). Footage profiles and output colour aren't scriptable, so the working space is the only lever.

destination.note: The audit's project.workingSpace check reads it back.

lessons.text: Start every nested layer 0.1 frame early: placed exactly on k x 1001/30000 s, AE showed the previous frame from one act on (picture 33 ms behind sound), and AE's own +-0.5-frame tolerance couldn't see it; check placement at 0.02 frame.

terms: a tenth of a frame early
destination.note: The audit checks every slice's start to 0.02 frame (engine/ae/validate.jsx).

terms: A sampling bias on nested comps

lessons.text: AE's stock "High Quality" output module is ProRes 422 (apcn), not 422 HQ, and neither ExtendScript nor the AE bridge can pick the codec inside an output module's format options: render the stock "High Quality with Alpha" (4444) and conform it to 422 HQ with ffmpeg's prores_ks.

terms: AE's stock "High Quality" output is ProRes 422, not 422 HQ

lessons.text: AE's disk cache filled 60 GB during one master: the masters job switches it off itself (refusing to start with AE open) and always restores the owner's setting afterwards, even on a failure or a kill; a watchdog stops the render under 4 GB free (masters peaked around 20 GB of disk). Emptying the cache is the owner's job, and Slate never deletes files outside the film folder.

terms: always put the previous value back
The disk cache is off while masters render
Emptying the cache is the owner's job

lessons.text: ffprobe prints AE QuickTime streams twice (a stream group); a shared frame-count helper takes the first integer.

terms: taking the first number ffprobe prints
ffprobe lists AE's movie streams twice

lessons.text: AE 26.5's AppleScript DoScript and DoScriptFile return 0 for every call, so scripts report through app.settings plus saveToDisk and a reader parses AE's prefs file; switch to JSON report files only when the file-write pref is on, keeping the settings channel as the fallback.

destination.note: AE 26.5 answers "0" to every DoScript, so scripts report through app.settings (read from the prefs file), or a JSON file when the preference is on (tests/ae/test_ae_driver.py::test_run_jsx_asks_for_a_file_report_only_when_the_pref_is_on).

lessons.text: AE project audit gate: 16 bpc, the working space matching the footage, linear blending off, shot comps matching shots.json to the frame (size, pixel aspect, fps, slice start within 0.02 frame), no placeholders or missing footage, act order, master frames, audio covering the film and markers, no missing or substituted fonts, no expression errors, and native motion blur on animated layers.

destination.note: One gate per audit check (slate.ae.audit.CHECKS: project.bpc, project.workingSpace, project.linearBlending, shots.comps, shots.picture, acts.comps, footage.missing, renders.format, master.frames, master.audio, master.markers, queue.chunks, fonts, expressions, motionblur.native); a check the report misses is UNCHECKED.

lessons.text: The ES3 library takes comp names, the act list and the film id as parameters instead of per-film wrapper scripts.

terms: pure: reads the film, writes nothing
destination.note: One ES3 library and one build script read a per-film spec (comp names, acts, film id), never a wrapper per film.

lessons.text: The AE master path depends on stock output-module template names and on toggling AE's disk-cache preference in a prefs file with AE closed, which is fragile across AE versions; doctor checks the templates exist and the prefs tool edits byte-safely.

destination.note: The audit fails a queue whose items don't each carry their two output modules; the smoke test records the templates aerender offers (details om_templates, rs_templates); the prefs tool edits byte-safely (tests/ae/test_ae_prefs.py). Doctor never launches AE, so it can't list templates itself.

terms: Proofs: identical outside the value, same line endings

lessons.text: SVG-to-AE shape conversion supports only M/L/H/V/C/Z path commands with translate and scale transforms; logos with arcs or other transforms must be flattened first.

destination.note: Superseded in Slate's favour: the converter reads every path command (arcs become cubics) and matrix transforms, so logos no longer need flattening.

lessons.text: AE cold-starts in about 41 s (about 1 s warm); the driver uses a 600 s AppleEvent timeout and takes the AE app name from config.

destination.note: AE cold-starts in about 41 s; the app name comes from AE_APP_NAME, then [ae] app, then the newest install.

lessons.text: Each host app that drives AE needs macOS Automation permission; the first call prompts and a denial shows as osascript error -1743, so doctor checks it from each real context (Claude Code, a Codex slice, the OpenClaw gateway).

destination.note: Checked per host app (the context doctor runs from); -1743 reads as denied.

lessons.text: One cross-process lock covers every route into AE (osascript scripts, the AE bridge, aerender): AE shows a blocking modal when a second script arrives mid-run, and a file write with the pref off can raise a modal that stalls the call.

destination.note: The same lock covers Slate's scripts, the bridge's busy lock and aerender (the job queue's `ae` slot).

terms: shared with the AE bridge's own busy lock

lessons.text: ExtendScript is ES3: var only, no JSON object, indexOf, forEach, map, trim or Object.keys, no trailing commas, each script an IIFE returning a string, properties addressed by match name, ease arrays sized to the property (1 for spatial, 3 for scale), and eases read back after they're set.

terms: each script an immediately invoked function returning a string
ease arrays sized to the property

lessons.text: Parse JSON inside AE with a vetted json2.jsx, not eval (eval is tolerable only for Slate's own generated JSON).

destination.note: Only JSON Slate wrote itself is parsed inside AE, after the RFC 4627 character check.

lessons.text: Set Mercury Software Only on footage-only AE projects: aerender crashed twice in the GPU compositor under memory pressure.

The AE bridge exchanges request and response files through a per-user mailbox and keeps its own busy lock (stale after 90 s); Slate's AE lock shares that lock so neither side runs a script while the other does.

destination.note: Slate's scripts take the bridge's busy lock in every candidate mailbox (slate.ae.bridgelock.hold).

lessons.text: Every bridge call runs inside one undo group, with default timeouts of 60 s (120 s to render a frame, 10 minutes to import).

destination.note: BridgeSession.timeout_for uses it: 60 s by default, 120 s to render a frame, 600 s to import, each plus a margin.

terms: Each call waits a little longer than the bridge's own limit for that tool

lessons.text: Doctor reports the AE bridge connected only after a live ae_project_info call succeeds; the bridge's own doctor checks files only.

destination.note: Green only once Slate's acceptance test (live calls against a scratch project) has passed on the pinned version; the bridge's own doctor checks files only.

lessons.text: Keep the bridge's arbitrary eval off, restrict its categories when a job needs only a few, and treat its mailbox folder as a code-execution trust boundary (write access to it runs code in AE).

destination.note: Every registration and session keeps arbitrary eval off and the categories limited (POLICY_ENV); the environment can't loosen it.

also.note: Mailboxes Slate creates are 0700 already.

terms: Its mailbox is a trust boundary

also.note: `slate connect aftereffects` registers the bridge with Claude Code the same way: eval off, the categories limited.

lessons.text: The bridge's frame render handles colour-managed projects with a transient display-transform layer and warns when it falls back; its frames aren't colour evidence unless that warning is clear.

terms: Its frame render handles colour-managed projects
aren't colour evidence unless that warning is clear

lessons.text: A queued render is not proof: check the output file exists with the expected template, bitrate and frame count.

destination.note: Every master is measured (frames, size, rate, sound), never trusted from the queue.

lessons.text: saveFrameToPng can silently drop files; verify every expected frame file exists after a frame export.

destination.note: Slate never exports frames with saveFrameToPng: AE frames come from an aerender render, pulled with ffmpeg and counted.

lessons.text: A timeout leaves an AE mutation's state unknown, and bridge batches aren't transactional: inspect the project before retrying any mutation.

terms: retried only when the project shows it didn't happen

lessons.text: Find AE's prefs folder by version sort, not text sort ('26.10' sorts before '26.5' as text).
Find AE and aerender by discovery (app bundle lookup), not a hard-coded, year-versioned path.

destination.note: AE and aerender are found under /Applications by bundle, newest first.

lessons.text: The master chunk count lives in one config value shared by the render-queue script and the masters runner; the films kept two copies that had to match by hand.

destination.note: One value ([ae] master_chunks, or --chunks) builds the plan both the queue script and the masters runner read from the spec.

lessons.text: Import vector logos into AE as editable shapes via PDF and 'Create Shapes from Vector Layer', looking the menu command up by name (its numeric id varies), in an empty project that's cleaned up afterwards.

destination.note: Logos arrive as native AE shape layers converted from the brand's SVG, so the PDF and "Create Shapes from Vector Layer" route isn't needed.

lessons.text: A generated clip was imported into an AE comp, titled on a brand ease, saved and rendered by aerender end to end during the toolchain proof.

terms: a toolchain proof imported a generated clip into an AE comp

lessons.text: A capability probe (colour API keys, TextDocument properties, output-module and render-settings templates, required effects by match name) runs in an empty project as part of doctor.

destination.note: The smoke test is the capability probe: a new AE version turns doctor's ae.app row yellow until it passes.

lessons.text: Shape-path keyframes interpolate a normalised 0-1 progress, so ease speed on a path is 1/T; AE also invalidates sibling property references after addProperty, so re-resolve them after every add.
Before any AE mutation, probe which project is open, whether it's dirty and what's in the render queue.

terms: whether it has unsaved changes, and the render queue's state

lessons.text: Purge AE's RAM caches before a long aerender (this doesn't touch the disk cache).

The ES3 library covers film-time snapping with the sample bias, eases converted to AE speed and influence with read-back, a settle-spring expression, shapes, text with per-character reveals, tabular counters, imports, plate layers, placeholders and a prefs-based report channel; brand tokens, fonts and names come from config.

destination.note: The ES3 library mirrors the Remotion kit: film-time snapping with the sample bias, eases as speed and influence read back, a settle-spring expression, shapes, text, counters, footage and placeholders, a prefs-based report channel.

terms: converted to AE speed and influence
Brand tokens, fonts (activated in AE, by PostScript name) and logo shapes come from the brand pack

lessons.text: Interpret generated plates at their native frame rate in AE, use Pixel Motion blending only on slow drifts, never add AE motion blur to them, and regenerate fast generated motion rather than time-stretching it.

destination.note: Footage layers never get AE motion blur; plates reach AE already conformed to film-rate sequences (the plate path).

terms: Generated footage gets no extra motion blur

lessons.text: The AE project uses a fixed folder layout (shots, acts, master, plates, audio, code renders) and tags every shot comp RENDERED, BUILT or PLACEHOLDER.

destination.note: The folders come from slate.ae.spec.FOLDERS; each shot comp is tagged by what fills it.

lessons.text: Native AE act builders (event-timed carriers from the film clock) proved AE can build scenes; they were superseded for one film but are the basis for AE-built acts.

terms: The first films' native AE act builders
they're the basis for AE-built acts

lessons.text: The master queue script reads each chunk's span back in frames and flags any mismatch before rendering.

terms: Every item's span is read back in frames

lessons.text: The disk watchdog stops only its own aerender, not every aerender on the machine (pkill -f aerender killed them all).
Shape layers default to an origin at the comp centre; set anchor and position to the centre to write comp-space vertices.

AE's launch-time dialogs (licence or sign-in, the Home screen, crash-recovery restore, missing fonts or footage on open) sit outside beginSuppressDialogs and can hang unattended runs; doctor detects them.

destination.note: Red rows naming the dialog, from the bridge's open_dialogs or AE's window titles (System Events; AE is never launched). Every supervised AE step runs launch_dialogs() once the person says go and stops on one (exit 5, naming it and the fix: slate.ae.guard.stop_on_dialogs), and `slate ae bridge status` reports open_dialogs.

also.note: AE steps start only on a person's go and masters run aerender with AE closed; doctor now reads AE's launch dialogs from its window titles and the bridge, without launching it (src/slate/doctor/aftereffects.py:launch_dialogs).
person_start runs it after the go: AE closed asks nothing; a dialog is Busy (exit 5) with its fix.
The bridge can't see a dialog, so its status reads AE's window titles (only while AE is open) and sorts them with doctor's classifier.

lessons.text: Adobe Media Encoder comes with AE and the bridge can queue to it, but the pipeline doesn't need it.

terms: Adobe Media Encoder comes with AE, but the pipeline doesn't need it

lessons.text: Doctor for AE checks presence and version, the aerender path, Automation permission, the scripting pref state, disk-cache state and free space, fonts from the brand pack, ffmpeg capabilities, Node and Remotion, the OCR engine, the Whisper model, MCP registration, and a live ae_project_info when the pref is on.

destination.note: Fonts, ffmpeg, Node and Remotion, OCR, Whisper and MCP registration are their own doctor rows.

lessons.text: Masters run with a preflight (AE GUI closed, disk cache off, free space of at least a few times the estimate) and a postflight (cache restored, manifest written last).

destination.note: The manifest is written last at delivery (slate deliver).

lessons.text: The AE bridge's project export and import use its own JSON schema, not Lottie; HTML-to-scene, cloud preview and a Lottie converter aren't provided.

terms: Its project export and import use its own JSON schema, not Lottie
it has no HTML-to-scene, cloud preview or Lottie converter

lessons.text: The vendor's AE panel and its cloud bridge generate footage into an AE project (CEP-based), a different route from the local bridge Slate uses; their automation targets repeated structured assignments, not complex character animation.

terms: The vendor's AE panel and cloud bridge

lessons.text: aerender renders without the AE interface; in Render-Only mode it reportedly doesn't need an Adobe sign-in (medium confidence).
aerender ignores its render-settings, output-module, output and range flags unless -comp is given.

destination.note: Masters render queue items, whose settings live in the saved project; the smoke test passes -comp with its own templates.

lessons.text: aerender's -mfr ON|OFF max_cpu_percent toggles Multi-Frame Rendering and caps CPU.
Several aerender instances can't write one movie file; parallel AE renders output image sequences, and plugins on render nodes carry their own licences.

terms: several aerender instances can't write one movie file
plug-ins on extra render machines carry their own licences

lessons.text: Build on ExtendScript (unaffected by Adobe's UXP move) and avoid CEP-panel routes for anything long-lived: AE's UXP beta is due by November 2026, and CEP leaves the flagship apps by December 2029.

terms: Build on ExtendScript, which Adobe's move to UXP doesn't affect

lessons.text: Community AE MCP servers (CEP-panel based, MIT) and nexrender (data-driven templates via aerender) exist as untested fallbacks.
Adobe's own AI (the in-app AE assistant, the Claude connector) can't drive After Effects; connecting to AE means a local bridge plus aerender.

terms: can't drive After Effects for an agent

lessons.text: After Effects steps start only on a person's go: Adobe's PSLT section 1.2 bars operations no individual user initiated (automated server processing, RPA) unless a Sales Order allows it, so autonomous mode never touches AE.

destination.note: Every AE step refuses without --go and for autonomous films (PSLT §1.2).

terms: AE steps start only on a person's go, and autonomous films never touch AE

lessons.text: The consumer General Terms for individual Creative Cloud subscriptions weren't reviewed; the PSLT rule applies until they are. Unlimited Render Engines are allowed on an intranet with one full AE install, and Media Encoder can't serve as a hosted encoder.

terms: Unlimited render engines are allowed on an intranet with one full AE install
Until the owner's own licence terms are checked

lessons.text: Never add output-module templates to the owner's AE preferences; the only preference Slate changes is the disk-cache toggle (with AE closed, restored afterwards) through the byte-safe prefs tool.

destination.note: The only preference Slate changes is the disk-cache toggle, through the byte-safe tool with AE closed.

terms: AE's preferences are changed only by Slate's byte-safe tool

lessons.text: The AE bridge's clean-rig references (one of them shaped the films' visual-foundation process) are worth reading through ae_get_skill during look development.

terms: The clean-rig references are worth reading during look development

lessons.text: Every shot gets an evidence set for review: a half-resolution motion preview with sound, strips of every frame from 10 before to 10 after each cut at full resolution, full-resolution detail frames on each event's landing frame and 20 frames after, and a motion scan.
Record each shot's QA status as pass, fixed -> pass, fail or pending, with notes; a human looks at the contact sheets and strips.
Film validation reports each check's state with its evidence, and nothing unchecked is ever reported as passed: a master's validation counts only once it has actually run.

destination.note: Only PASS counts; UNCHECKED and STALE exist so a check that didn't run can't pass.

lessons.text: Log every defect with measured evidence (for example a 17.8 px jump at frame 1166, or a join jump of 1.36 against 0.13) and its fix, and move the shot's status to fixed -> pass.

terms: Log every defect with measured evidence and its fix

lessons.text: Validation report template: check, result and evidence per row, with a detail section for each failure.

destination.note: `slate qa triage` lists every result that isn't PASS with its evidence and next step; qa/gates.json holds each gate's latest result, and delivery copies it (slate.finish.deliver).

lessons.text: One banned-word list per brand is enforced at every layer: the script gate, the act files at hand-in, OCR of the rendered picture at full width, the captions and the transcript of the voice; a banned word is never set on screen.

destination.note: Script, captions and OCR of the picture read the pack's one list; the act files are checked at hand-in; the voice's transcript isn't matched yet (L-qa-D012); brand assets aren't scanned or quarantined (generated plates never carry text).

lessons.text: A frame-glitch scanner flags smooth fast motion (anything over about 3 px/frame); build triage into the check with a ratio test or motion-compensated matching, and skip flags within +-3 frames of a planned beat.

destination.note: Flags within ±3 frames of a planned beat are listed as skipped; the ratio and motion-compensated triage are L-qa-D048's gap.

terms: flags within 3 frames of a planned beat are skipped

lessons.text: Every validator takes the film folder and reads only that film's files: one film's first validation read another film's captions and old cue sheets, and passed the wrong film.

destination.note: Every gate is a function of the film folder, read through one FilmContext; the tests run every gate on two films side by side and prove each reads only its own.

also.note: Every gate is a function of the film folder, read through one FilmContext.

terms: Validators read the film they validate

lessons.text: A read-time checker needs the text as drawn: most read-time failures on one film (9 of 10) were checker faults. Keep the script's on-screen text identical to what's drawn, let the matcher forgive one garbled first word, and leave tiny labels and logo lockups (OCR reads a mark as stray letters) to contact-sheet review.

terms: labels are left to the contact-sheet review
Logo lockups and stylized marks are left to the contact-sheet review

lessons.text: Read time on the master: OCR every 0.25 s at full output width finds each on-screen statement inside its shot (±0.5 s), counts it only once it's fully built (in order, with its last word; a fuzzy match of at least 0.9), and holds its longest legible run to max(1.5 s, 0.4 s + 0.3 s per word) from the frame it settles, with one OCR interval of slack.

destination.note: Legibility is read by OCR; opacity and motion aren't measured separately (L-qa-D043).

lessons.text: Read-time extras: numbers and statistics hold at least 2.0 s after their count lands; labels of three words or fewer hold at least 1.0 s; a line the voice also says stays on screen at least as long as the voice takes to say it, and never leaves before the voice finishes it.

destination.note: The script gate plans the 2 s number hold; the label and voice-matched rules are skill rules, and the master's readtime gate adds neither (see the GAPS.md appendix).

terms: Labels of three words or fewer

lessons.text: Motion scan: a frame-to-frame difference spike (the films used over max(8, 6 × (median + 0.5)) and 2.5 times both neighbours) that isn't within ±3 frames of a planned event or a shot edge is flagged for a person.

destination.note: The glitch scan (tile scores, ±3-frame beat triage, REVIEW for the rest) does this job on every act render.

lessons.text: Cuts gate: no hard cuts or crossfades between shots; allowed boundaries are a carry, portal, mask, motion-masked whip, a UI state cut with the camera locked, or at most three cuts on musical hits; a detected scene change (ffmpeg scene > 0.33) must sit within 3 frames of a shot start whose transition allows it, else REVIEW.

destination.note: ffmpeg scene score over 0.33 (slate.analyze.cuts); a declared carry, portal, mask, whip, ui_cut, at most three music_cuts, or a seam of 4 frames or less allows its cut.

also.note: Stated as the law; the cuts gate checks every act render's scene changes and joins against the declared transitions.

terms: How the shot hands to the next: a carry, a portal, a mask, a whip
also.note: Each shot's transition is data in script.json; the cuts gate sorts it into the law's kinds (slate.qa.checks.picture.TRANSITIONS).

terms: Every scene change is a carry, a portal, a mask, a whip or an allowed exception
whose declared transition allows a cut

lessons.text: Join gate: across every act join, the jump must not exceed the largest frame step within 10 frames either side plus 1.0 (mean absolute difference, 0 to 255), with the strip saved as evidence; a gap or overlap fails. Contract holds are at least 6 still frames each side.

destination.note: The 6-frame holds are the hand-in contracts gate's (handin.act<N>.contracts). Its golden test (tests/qa_core/test_qa_core_golden.py::test_golden_boundary_reproduces_film_a_delivered_joins, opt-in with SLATE_GOLDEN_HEAVY=1) skips until the film session regenerates film A's boundary report: the report is older than A's renders since they were re-rendered.

lessons.text: Glitch gate: decode every render small (480 × 270 luma), score each 16 × 9 tile as min(d(n−1, n), d(n, n+1)) − d(n−1, n+1)/2 over 1- and 2-frame windows, flag frames over 6.0 that differ from both neighbours while the neighbours agree, then triage against planned beats.
Master fidelity gate: every master frame is at least 40 dB PSNR against the act render it came from, with an exact frame count (one film averaged 56.5 dB, worst 51.6 dB).

destination.note: Every master frame against the act renders at 40 dB or better, every frame there.

terms: every frame, at the film's PSNR bar

lessons.text: Media gate: ProRes 422 HQ and H.264 masters at the film's size and fps, exact frame count, with audio present.

destination.note: Every master is measured for frames, size, rate and sound; the codec follows from how masters are made (ProRes 422 HQ and H.264) and isn't re-read.

lessons.text: Captions gate: the captions reproduce the script word for word, every cue and word; at most 2 lines of 42 characters; each cue at least 1.0 s; never overlapping; shown from its first word to its last word plus 0.35 s.

Spoken-words gate: Whisper (model recorded in the evidence) on the final mix against the booth script, under 5% unmatched else REVIEW, the brand name heard in full as many times as scripted, and no banned words in the transcript.

destination.note: Whisper hears every take in use against the script (brand words in full, model recorded); the mix is proven to be those takes by stems_sum and the sync gate's voice placement, so no second Whisper pass runs on the mix.

lessons.text: QA tools read the brand word, banned list, targets and film folder from the brand pack and film.json; the films hard-coded one brand's words, a reference runtime and film switches.

destination.note: The banned list, targets and folders come from the brand pack and film.json (tests/qa_core/test_qa_core_regressions.py::test_regression_no_banned_list_lives_in_the_qa_code).

lessons.text: One film's last validation showed word-landing failures (93 beats, worst 469.7 ms) with its re-master pending.

destination.reason: A status of one film when it was read (its word landings awaiting a re-master), not a lesson; the sync gate that caught it is in the ledger.

lessons.text: Record the Whisper model in every gate's evidence (turbo for per-take timing, large-v3-turbo for the final transcript).

terms: the model and its version are recorded in the evidence

lessons.text: Delete OCR frames once their JSON is cached (keyed by file size and mtime), and delete verified intermediates (4444 chunks, chunk files) straight away.

destination.note: The sweep decodes frames in memory a few at a time and keeps only the text (cached in qa/ocr/); masters delete each verified 4444 chunk straight away (slate.ae.masters).

lessons.text: A quick validation mode skips the slow checks (read-time OCR, Whisper) for iteration, but only a full run can pass delivery.

destination.note: `--quick` skips them, and a skipped gate is never a pass (tests/qa_core/test_qa_core_text.py::test_quick_mode_never_starts_the_sweep).

lessons.text: The loudness check must actually gate 24-bit output: an operator-precedence bug left its result unused, so bit depth was reported but never gated.
Treat a stem at or below -69.9 LUFS, or with no true peak, as silent: ebur128 floors silence at -70.0, so a '< -70' test never fired and an empty ambience stem passed.
One OCR engine (Apple Vision through the Python environment) serves every gate; when it's unavailable the gate is UNCHECKED, never a quiet pass from another engine.

destination.note: tests/qa_core/test_qa_core_text.py::test_ocr_is_unchecked_without_vision_and_never_falls_back.

terms: OCR gates use Apple Vision only

lessons.text: Vision's accurate recognition may be missing its model assets; doctor checks which level is available and gates record the level they used.

destination.note: Doctor names the recognition level that runs; every OCR result records it (tests/qa_core/test_qa_core_text.py::test_ocr_level_is_recorded_not_quietly_changed).

lessons.text: OCR runs on full-output-width frames only; at 1280 px it misread letter-spaced capitals (an 'I' read as a '1', a 'B' as an '8').

destination.note: The sweep reads each frame at the film's own width.

lessons.text: The owner's ponder skill (converging grading passes) can run as a QA loop over every shot.

terms: Ponder: a QA loop over every shot

lessons.text: Freeze, flash and blank-frame metrics (as in video-verifier's analyzer) belong in Slate's QA beside the glitch scan.

destination.note: Reported by the glitch gate (src/slate/qa/checks/picture.py:glitch) as REVIEW items with their film frames, triaged against planned beats; flashes are the access gate's.

lessons.text: Captions stay at or under 17 characters per second (Netflix's children's limit; 20 for adults), with each caption event between 5/6 s and 7 s.

destination.note: At most 17 characters a second; each cue at least 1.0 s (stricter than 5/6 s); the 7 s maximum isn't checked.

lessons.text: On-screen text never straddles a cut.

destination.reason: Superseded by Slate's own read-time rule (skills/slate-motion/references/read-time.md): a statement may ride a deliberate camera move across a cut as long as it stays legible there, so a blanket ban doesn't hold for supers.

lessons.text: Keep titles inside title-safe (90% of the frame: 1728x972 at 1080p, 96 px in from the sides and 54 px from top and bottom) and action inside 93%; social formats add their platform safe zones.

also.note: Platform zones and the general title-safe box are both gated (the access gate reads them by OCR).

lessons.text: At most three flashes a second (WCAG 2.3.1).
Building the Vision OCR helper from Swift source at install.

destination.reason: Superseded: the plan keeps one OCR engine (Apple Vision through ocrmac, installed with uv) and drops the Swift helper.

lessons.text: The validation report's check table doubles as the delivery gate spec.

destination.note: The gates delivery requires are one list, read by `slate deliver`.

lessons.text: Events gate: every act in shots.json has a valid events file or an explicit silent flag with a reason; one film's first two acts had no events file, yet its sync check passed.
The banned-word list is defined once per brand and imported by every check; one validator kept its own copy of the list, which could drift from the script gate's.
The act-join check runs on any film's renders; the source tool was hard-wired to one film.
Contact sheets every 0.5 s, labelled with timecode, are made straight from the act renders.

destination.note: A frame every 0.5 s (review.sheet_step_s), tiled and labelled with frame, shot and timecode, made from the act renders or the master.

lessons.text: Delivery includes the masters, stems, captions, a SHA-256 manifest of every deliverable (missing ones listed), review and phone cuts, contact sheets, a rebuild runbook, an asset ledger with provenance and spend, and QA records.

destination.note: deliver/vN/: masters, the mix and its stems, captions, review and phone cuts, contact sheets, thumbnails, the AE project, synthetic-media flags, the gates' results, and the manifest last (every file's bytes, SHA-256 and probe, missing ones listed). Rebuilding comes from the film folder itself (see L-finish-006).

lessons.text: Make share-size copies for the owner as part of delivery: a full H.264, a copy small enough for chat (about 70 MB) and a phone copy.

destination.note: Code: review packets go to the owner's Downloads (finish/review.py) with the phone cut; the delivery set carries the half-size review cut and the phone cut.

lessons.text: When more than one mix exists, an audio README states which one is the delivery.

destination.note: A Slate delivery holds exactly one mix (the final mix, its record and the delivery stems), named in the manifest; superseded mixes live in the film's archive/, so there's nothing to disambiguate.

lessons.text: Review cuts at every stage: voice-only previews, per-shot half-res previews with sound, whole-film half-res and phone cuts with contact sheets straight from act renders, and side-by-side comparisons (code versus generated, alternative versus flagship).
Rebuild runbook template: tools and versions, locked inputs not to regenerate, picture per act, sound, AE and masters, and checks; a film must rebuild from its folder with no paid generation.

destination.note: A film rebuilds from its own folder: film.lock.json records what made every file, pins keep models and voices, approved paid assets are locked by hash, and `slate make all` rebuilds only what's stale without paying again. No REBUILD.md is written: the folder is the runbook.

lessons.text: Never mux with ffmpeg -shortest: it cut the last 4 frames because the mix was 9 microseconds short; write mixes exactly picture length and verify frame counts after every mux.
Output names (masters, captions, review cuts, manifests) derive from the film id, not a hard-coded film name.

destination.note: Every output name comes from the film's own id and version.

lessons.text: Contact sheets, burst sheets and labelled sheets use a bundled or configured font, never a macOS system font path.

destination.note: The configured font first; otherwise a system font if one is found, else Pillow's built-in font: never a hard-coded path.

lessons.text: Formats carry their loudness target (web about -14 LUFS, broadcast -23 or -24 LUFS) instead of one hard-coded target.

destination.note: Each format carries its loudness target; a broadcast format sets its own (formats/_platforms.json names EBU R 128 and ATSC A/85).

lessons.text: Join master chunks by stream copy (H.264 chunks start on an IDR frame; ProRes is intra-only), then mux the final mix once: AAC 320 kb/s at 48 kHz with faststart for H.264, 24-bit PCM for ProRes.

destination.note: Chunks join by stream copy and the mix is muxed once: AAC 320k at 48 kHz for H.264, 24-bit PCM for ProRes.

lessons.text: Review cut: 960x540 at about 3 Mb/s with 192k AAC; phone cut: 640x360 at about 450 kb/s with 96k AAC and under 30 MB; contact sheets: a frame every 0.5 s at 480x270, 12x10 per sheet, labelled m:ss.s.

destination.note: Slate's defaults: a half-size review cut at up to 3 Mb/s with 192k AAC, a phone cut 360 px on its short side with 96k AAC, contact sheets every 0.5 s in 12 x 10 grids.

lessons.text: Write the delivery manifest last: it hashes files, so anything regenerated after it (a validation report, for example) leaves a stale hash.

destination.note: The manifest is written after everything else in the set, so nothing regenerated afterwards can leave it stale.

also.note: Enforced by construction (the manifest is written after everything else) and tested: tests/finish/test_finish_deliver.py::test_manifest_is_written_last_with_every_hash. Harvest proposed a gate; the order is fixed in code instead.

lessons.text: The manifest lists every deliverable with bytes, SHA-256 and an ffprobe summary, and lists missing ones instead of skipping them.
Derived cut-downs (9:16, 1:1) and a -16 LUFS web alternative were planned for the films but never scripted; in Slate they're derived films with their own gates.

destination.note: Cut-downs, new aspects and new languages are derived films (slate new --parent --derivation), each with its own gates and approval.

lessons.text: The local ffmpeg build has no drawtext, subtitles or libass, so labels are drawn with Pillow and captions are burned in by the renderer.

destination.note: Labels burn in with ffmpeg's drawtext when the build has it, else Pillow; captions are burned in by the renderer.

lessons.text: Thumbnails and covers can come from the generation vendor's thumbnail skill at delivery.

terms: A vendor's thumbnail tool can make covers

lessons.text: Held films and questions reach the owner by iMessage (with the phone cut) and push notification, the channels Oneiro already uses for asks.

destination.note: Held films and questions go by iMessage with the phone cut and as a push (never in tests or replay).

lessons.text: A web-embedded film longer than 5 s needs a pause, stop or hide control on the page (WCAG 2.2.2); the website hero-loop format notes it.
YouTube's -14 LUFS target is lore, not a documented spec; choose platform targets deliberately and verify with ffmpeg.

The vendor's timeline editor suits fast, timing-exact variants (social cut-downs, re-timed or re-voiced versions, animatics) driven by the same events and word timings, not the flagship (no 3D, limited motion blur, no visual editing); it's benchmarked against a Remotion cut-down before adoption.

terms: it suits variants, not the flagship

lessons.text: Snapshot every vendor's credit balance at the toolchain proof and at the start and end of each paid session, so spend can be reconciled by difference.
Run finals one at a time from a queue: six builders plus 16-sample renders once drove the load average to 293 on 14 cores.

destination.note: One render slot by default (render.slots = 1) and the runner's load guard keep finals one at a time.

lessons.text: A credit-heavy optional extra (for example a dedicated score swell costing about 1,100-1,500 credits) is offered with its price and made only on the owner's explicit yes.

terms: An optional extra that costs real credits
made only on the owner's yes, even when the budget would cover it
An optional extra that costs real credits

lessons.text: Never edit a shell script while a job runs it: zsh reads scripts incrementally and a job failed at its last line; run jobs from a copied, versioned script.

terms: Never edit a shell script while a job is running it

lessons.text: Record the character-cost response header of every ElevenLabs call in the ledger.
File locks stop a watcher and a manual run from writing the same mix or score at once.

destination.note: One writer per mix: a second run refuses while the lock is held; the queue's resource locks do the same across jobs.

lessons.text: Watchers hash inputs portably (in Python, not md5 -q or ls -lT) and tolerate missing act files.

destination.note: Inputs are hashed in Python (sha256), and a missing input hashes to None (stale), never a crash; film.lock.json replaces the zsh watchers.

lessons.text: Service concurrency limits bite (2 concurrent music requests on one plan, about 4 generation jobs on another before 429): use per-service worker counts with retry and backoff.

destination.note: Per-service slots; vendor rate limits make a job exit 75 so the queue retries it later.

lessons.text: A six-minute film's masters take about 11.6 GB (H.264 about 1.7 GB, ProRes 422 HQ about 9.8 GB) and peak around 20 GB of disk while rendering; reserve that before starting.

destination.note: The master reserves disk from the renders' real sizes before it starts (slate.jobs.disk).

lessons.text: ElevenLabs API concurrency by plan: Free 2, Starter 3, Creator 5, Pro 10, Scale and Business 15; music has its own lower limit (2 at once on one plan).

destination.note: The per-plan table itself is in knowledge/registry_proposal.json (providers.elevenlabs.concurrency) for the integrator to merge into registry.json.

lessons.text: Generations through the hosted connector always deduct credits whatever the plan ('unlimited' applies only in the web UI) and bypass Slate's ledger, so the ledger reconciles balance snapshots at the start and end of each session.
Paid vendor calls print a cost estimate and refuse to spend without an explicit confirmation or a budget that covers them, so no agent burns credits by accident.
A 1-second smoke render took about 7 s (27 s including engine launch), and a six-minute master took 8 chunks of about 55-90 s each.

destination.reason: A one-off timing on one Mac, not a rule: the queue shows every job's real elapsed time (slate job status), and the After Effects timeouts (600 s for the smoke test, 30 minutes or 5 s a frame per master chunk) sit well above it.

lessons.text: One brand film used about 76,600 ElevenLabs credits through production on a 131,000-credit monthly plan; default budgets come from that kind of measured spend.

destination.note: Default budgets come from what the films measurably spent (formats/_shared.json budgets.source).

lessons.text: Run one MCP client instance per tool at a time: two copies of one plugin ran every create twice and left duplicates.

destination.note: Command lines are never reported; two scripts sent to After Effects at once are prevented by the shared AE lock (slate.ae.bridgelock).

terms: One copy of any MCP client at a time
also.note: Doctor's agents.mcp.single-instance row reports two copies of one server under one client; the collision that matters most (two scripts sent to After Effects) is also prevented in code by the shared AE lock (slate.ae.bridgelock).

lessons.text: Register the AE bridge per agent with its own installers: claude mcp add for Claude, fnf-after-effects install-codex for Codex, and the fnf-after-effects config output for OpenClaw.

Five skill roots (Claude Code's, the shared ~/.agents root, Codex's legacy root, OpenClaw's managed root and claude.ai account skills) were kept in sync by hand-copying and had already drifted; Slate installs by symlink from one checkout.

destination.note: Slate's skills are symlinked from one checkout into each agent's root; a copy is flagged as drift (doctor agents.skills.*).

lessons.text: ~/.agents/skills is the one directory both Codex and OpenClaw read; Claude Code doesn't read it but follows symlinks in ~/.claude/skills.
Every capability works from a shell (CLI-first); MCP is a convenience layer, because pursuit research slices ignore user MCP config and get only the injected Aside and Apple servers.

terms: so the CLI is the contract and MCP is a convenience

lessons.text: Every vendor stage calls the vendor's REST API from Slate's own code with keys from the environment or the Keychain; the hosted connectors only reach Claude's chat surfaces, and Codex and OpenClaw have neither.

destination.note: Vendor stages call the REST APIs from Slate's own clients (slate.vendors.elevenlabs, slate.vendors.higgsfield) with keys from slate.secrets (environment, then Keychain).

lessons.text: Claude chat and Cowork load only account-level skills, not ~/.claude/skills; Slate uploads a knowledge-only skill to the account for them.

Claude chat runs in a cloud sandbox and Cowork in a VM, so neither can run AE, aerender, osascript or local ffmpeg; chat plans, writes and voices, and starts renders only through Slate's local desktop extension.

terms: starts renders only through the extension

lessons.text: Doctor flags agent instructions that allow any browser other than Aside; one agent's global instructions still endorsed driving the owner's personal browser.
Codex runs here with approvals off and a full-access sandbox, so Slate enforces its own guardrails (spend, browser, AE) in code instead of relying on agent prompts.

destination.note: Guardrails live in code: BROWSER=none on every child (slate.procs), spend refused by the ledger (slate.ledger.check_budget), After Effects refused for autonomous films (slate.ae.guard).

lessons.text: In OpenClaw, skill roots follow a precedence (workspace skills, workspace .agents/skills, ~/.agents/skills with the default state dir, ~/.openclaw/skills, workshop, bundled, extra dirs), MCP tools surface as server__tool, and the Claude CLI backend wraps selected skills as a temporary plugin.

destination.note: Slate installs into ~/.agents/skills, which OpenClaw reads with its default state folder; the precedence and tool-naming facts sit behind that choice.

lessons.text: Register Slate's MCP server in OpenClaw itself, not in a Codex home: the per-agent Codex home has no MCP servers and a wildcard tool deny likely puts Codex-harness turns in restricted mode.
Announce Slate to OpenClaw agents through the skill's own name and description, not AGENTS.md (at 19,927 of its 20,000-character injection cap) or TOOLS.md (no longer injected).

terms: Slate announces itself to OpenClaw agents through its skill's own name and description

lessons.text: Slate's CLI reads keys itself (environment, then Keychain), so it doesn't depend on OpenClaw's secret store, whose egress allowlist lacks the ElevenLabs and Higgsfield hosts.
The CLI is also linked into /opt/homebrew/bin, because the OpenClaw gateway's PATH doesn't include ~/.local/bin; restart the gateway after installing.

destination.note: The CLI is linked into ~/.local/bin and /opt/homebrew/bin; the OpenClaw entries tell the person to restart the gateway (skills_build.openclaw_entries).

lessons.text: Pursuit research slices run codex exec with user config ignored and model-provider keys stripped, but still load skills from HOME, so Slate reaches them as a skill plus a CLI and never needs those keys.

Oneiro's strategist and composeBrief need one video capability line (filed as a self-want, never an engine edit) before pursuits plan video work; an eval then dry-runs the strategist on a pursuit snapshot and expects a Slate move.

destination.note: The eval case oneiro-strategist-slate-move stays pending until Oneiro's self-want lands; the grader and the pending rule are tested.

lessons.text: Agents run on different models (Codex's default gpt-6-astra, pursuit slices on gpt-6-sol, deployed agents on gpt-5.6-sol), and gpt-6-astra is a model id, not a separate agent; evals cover each configuration.

destination.note: The eval matrix runs every configuration the plan names; its test holds the models and setups to the plan.

also.note: tests/evals/test_evals_suite_files.py::test_models_and_setups_match_the_plan holds the four configurations to the plan.

lessons.text: The owner's visionary and goal-fidelity skills were Claude-only, missing from Codex, OpenClaw and pursuit slices; they get their own shareable repo symlinked into every personal agent.

destination.note: Their own small repo, symlinked into every personal agent with the owner's one-time yes (scripts/setup_quinn_skills.sh).

lessons.text: Frontend taste skill sets fanned out to many agent folders, and Oneiro's agent-learned marketing skills, aren't video skills.

destination.reason: Not part of Slate: other skill sets stay exactly where their owners put them (PLAN section 1, "Your other personal skills stay exactly as they are").

lessons.text: Skills that move renders between the owner's two Macs, and a map of the machines, are private topology.

destination.reason: Private machine topology, and renders are now local only (ARCHITECTURE section 1, rule 9): nothing about moving renders between machines belongs in a shareable core.

lessons.text: mac-cua is optional for dismissing AE dialogs and background app control; its browser tools are never used.
Never call the generation connector's sync_agents tool: it uploads the user's skills and a personality profile to the vendor, including machine topology and company taste.

destination.note: No code path calls the denied tool; the scan fails if one appears outside the denial list. No eval grader looks for it in a transcript yet.

also.note: Enforced by a scan: tests/gencap/test_gencap_scan.py::test_denied_connector_tools_exist_nowhere_but_in_denials and ::test_the_higgsfield_client_has_no_connector_tools. No eval grader looks for it in a transcript yet.

lessons.text: Aside is the only browser: every Slate child process runs with BROWSER=none and Remotion Studio with --no-open, so no tool can open the owner's personal browser.
An eval checks that no browser other than Aside is ever launched.
Company-ops MCP servers are off-limits to Slate.
The generation vendor's CLI signs in through a browser OAuth flow that the owner runs in their own Terminal; an agent never starts it.
Autonomous mode spends only with the actuator's approval id or a budget envelope granted to the pursuit, since Oneiro's committing actions go through its risk gate.
Oneiro's evidence must quote a re-readable file or an Aside-captured page, so Slate's outputs are files at stable paths with JSON status.
One pursuit's goal, workstreams and dated milestones.

destination.reason: One pursuit's own goal and dated milestones: context for that pursuit, not a lesson.

lessons.text: Two Codex binaries are in use (the npm CLI and the one bundled with the ChatGPT app, which runs the pursuits), and both read ~/.agents/skills and ~/.codex/skills: install Slate's skills into ~/.agents/skills only, or Codex lists each twice (it was already happening for three skills). Doctor checks each Slate skill appears exactly once.
ElevenLabs' hosted MCP is OAuth-only with regional residency endpoints; it's the chat lane, while pipelines and headless agents call the API with a key through the SDK or CLI.

terms: never for pipelines or headless agents

lessons.text: The generation vendor's hosted MCP uses browser OAuth and suits chat clients; the vendor itself points Claude Code, OpenClaw and Hermes to its CLI and skills instead.

terms: points agents such as Claude Code and OpenClaw to its CLI and skills

lessons.text: On claude.ai, a plugin's skills load in chat and Cowork, agents and hooks load only in Cowork and Code, remote MCP servers appear on the Connectors tab, and local or .mcpb servers load only in a locally running Cowork session.

terms: A plugin's skills load in chat and Cowork

lessons.text: Custom remote connectors on claude.ai authenticate by OAuth (or beta request headers), their auth settings can't be edited after adding, and they're reached through Anthropic's infrastructure.
Codex scans skills from the working directory's .agents/skills up to the repo root, then ~/.agents/skills, /etc/codex/skills and bundled skills, following symlinks; colliding names both appear.

destination.note: Codex's scan order is why Slate links into ~/.agents/skills and never ~/.codex/skills.

lessons.text: Codex MCP servers go in ~/.codex/config.toml (stdio or HTTP with bearer-token env vars, startup and tool timeouts); a project's .codex/config.toml applies only in trusted projects.

destination.note: Registration goes through `codex mcp add` (the user config), never a project file.

lessons.text: Codex loads AGENTS.md files from ~/.codex and from the git root down to the working directory, concatenated, with a 32 KiB cap by default.

terms: Loads AGENTS.md files from its home and from the git root down

lessons.text: OpenClaw skill env and apiKey values reach host runs only, not the sandbox, and requires.bins is checked on the host.

terms: Skill env and API-key values reach host runs only

lessons.text: OpenClaw MCP servers live under mcp.servers in openclaw.json (stdio, or a URL with streamable-http or SSE, headers, OAuth, tool filters and timeouts), managed with 'openclaw mcp set'.
Codex installs Slate from the Agent Plugins manifest with codex plugin marketplace add; the fallback is symlinks into ~/.agents/skills plus codex mcp add.

destination.note: The fallback route: symlinks into ~/.agents/skills plus `codex mcp add`; the Agent Plugins route is plugins/slate (README).

lessons.text: OpenClaw reads ~/.agents/skills only when its state dir is the default; the owner's gateway uses the default, so Slate's symlink there works, and doctor checks visibility from the gateway context.
The generation vendor's skills were installed for Claude only; Slate's installer also installs them for Codex and OpenClaw, with the owner's one-time yes.
MCP servers unrelated to film-making (a website builder, a ticket tracker, a company sidecar, Oneiro's memory, the Apple broker, Codex's own tooling, bio-research servers) aren't part of Slate.

destination.reason: Nothing to carry: those servers are simply not part of Slate (PLAN appendix A, "Not part of Slate"); the company ones are also off-limits (L-agents-027).

lessons.text: Doctor must prove ffmpeg can actually encode, not just that the binary exists: the first install had a broken x265 library and failed only when used.

destination.note: Doctor runs ffmpeg and fails one whose libraries won't load (the films' broken x265); it doesn't run a test encode.

lessons.text: Evaluate suggested tools quickly and record the verdict with reasons; installs that need system permissions go to the owner (one repo 404'd, one had no file output and would open a browser, one needed macOS permissions).

terms: Checking a tool before anyone installs it
Record the verdict with reasons in the tracker
Installs that need system permissions go to the owner

lessons.text: Website project artifacts that shared the film folder (handoff and context docs, component library and audit, Framer tooling, site deliverables).

destination.reason: A separate project's material (the website build that shared the film folder), not part of the film pipeline; the plan leaves the website tooling behind.

lessons.text: Secrets are referenced by name only (a Keychain item, an env var, an OAuth login, an MCP connection) and their values are never printed, logged or written.

destination.note: Keys are named (an env var, a Keychain item); values never leave the resolver (slate.secrets.redact).

terms: never printed, logged, written to a file or put in a URL

lessons.text: Declare every dependency the engine uses (esbuild ran every emitter but was undeclared), remove declared-but-unused ones (framer-motion, @remotion/motion-blur, postprocessing, @react-three/postprocessing), and keep package scripts pointing at files that exist.

destination.note: Declared; the unused packages are gone (engine/tests/core/cli.test.mjs checks both).

lessons.text: Never read an API key out of another client's config file; resolve keys only through Slate's secrets module.

destination.note: Keys resolve only through slate.secrets (the environment, then the Keychain), never from another client's config.

lessons.text: Pin engines: the source Mac ran Node 26 and Python 3.14, newer than most agent environments, so Slate declares the Node and Python versions it supports.

lessons.text: Masters render in chunks (8 for a six-minute film): the master comp is queued as one item per chunk with two stock output modules (H.264 and ProRes 4444) so one pass writes both, each chunk in a fresh aerender (`-mem_usage 25 50`; one long aerender grew until the Mac swapped and aborted) with AE's interface quit first, up to three tries, resuming by frame count. Nothing runs alongside aerender: each 4444 chunk is conformed to 422 HQ with prores_ks after its pass, its frames checked and the 4444 deleted; the chunks join by stream copy and the final mix is muxed in.

terms: The masters render with aerender in chunks: each chunk in a fresh process

A half-frame tolerance couldn't see it; only a frame-by-frame comparison of the master against the renders did, and the same check caught AE converting colour (a deep brand colour 8 levels dark, fixed by the Rec.709 Gamma 2.4 working space).

terms: a tenth of a frame early

Glitch triage by ratio and motion compensation. For a flagged frame n, r = d(n−1, n+1) / min(d(n−1, n), d(n, n+1)), plus the share of changed pixels where n lies between its neighbours; calibrated on the films, flashes and flickers score r ≤ 0.21, layers passing through each other 0.38 to 0.44 and smooth motion 0.55 to 0.80 and above. Block-match each flag against its neighbours: shifted neighbours explaining it is fast motion, nothing moving is an in-place change, anything else is checked by eye. A clean text pan flags from about 4 px a frame at 1920 wide and a clean zoom from about 0.5% a frame even with 180-degree blur, so an untriaged scan can pass only slow content.

destination.note: Wired into the glitch gate through slate.qa.stability.explain_glitches; open flags keep r, the between share and the match in their evidence.

lessons.text: No question rise: a take's last word may rise at most 3 semitones past the voice's untagged endings of that line (a fall never counts as a rise); a one-word declarative that rises 6.6 semitones reads as a question.

destination.note: The film gate caps a statement ending at the voice's own endings plus 3 semitones; the tag loop's ending gate does the same against the untagged takes of the line.

terms: the last word rises at most 3 semitones past the untagged endings

lessons.text: Complete: a take must not stop mid-word. Its last 20 ms sit at least 35 dB under its speech level; the clipped takes ended only 10 to 16 dB down, where the voice's untagged takes end 47 dB or more down.

Creak: a take may creak no more than the voice's untagged takes of the line plus one percentage point. Creak is voiced frames under the lower of 115 Hz and 0.6 times the take's median pitch, or pitch more than 20% off a 5-frame running median, with the words it falls on.

destination.note: A take of a tag round that creaks more than the untagged reads plus a point is out; no test drives a creaky take yet, and the film's inflection gate reports creak as a note.

terms: no more creak than the untagged reads, plus one point

lessons.text: Measure a line's intended emotion on its emotion words against the voice's untagged takes of the same words, with one proxy per intent: a smile is pitch up 0.8 to 3.5 semitones (past that reads theatrical) and brighter (centroid +4% or F2 +2%, F2 only on spans with 80+ voiced frames); reassurance or sincerity is a steadier pitch (F0 SD at least 0.2 semitones lower) or 3% slower at full level; a hopeful last word lifts at least 0.5 semitones more than untagged, fully voiced, level held. Among takes that pass every gate, the pick shows the clearest shift, with fullness of voice in its favour. These are measurements; the owner picks by ear.

destination.note: Each intent is measured on its emotion span against the untagged reads of the same words; the pick is the clearest feeling with the fullest voice.

lessons.text: Measure each direction tag on each voice instead of trusting its word: on one designed voice "with a smile" reliably added fullness, while "sincere", "kind", "warm" and "reassuring" made it measurably breathier (mostly through H1-H2) and plain, steady words ("candid, steady", "matter-of-fact") kept its own voice.

terms: Some tags make a voice breathier even when they sound harmless
a smile made the same voice fuller

lessons.text: The seed changes a tagged take's verdict as much as the tag does (one tag passed on one seed of four, and a winning text lost its lift on a new seed): judge exact takes, and use an approved take as that exact file, never regenerated.

terms: The seed matters as much as the tag
destination.note: Several seeds per candidate, and the pick goes in as that exact file (slate.voice.tagloop.adopt).

terms: never re-voiced in the hope of getting it back

lessons.text: A mid-line smile tag can make the model say the next phrase twice even after a short-pause tag; Whisper catches the repeat, and the clean take is kept rather than regenerated.

destination.note: Whisper hears every take word for word: a repeat fails the take; the clean take is kept rather than regenerated.

terms: a word-for-word check on every take

lessons.text: Uncorrected H1-H2 rises as the pitch climbs toward the vowel's first formant, so a lifted word can read breathy on H1-H2 while its voicing, CPPS, HNR and tilt all read fuller: judge a lifted word by the breath index, not by H1-H2 alone.

destination.note: The verdict is the mean of six measures' z (or two core measures over 1.5, or the voice dropping out), so H1-H2 rising with a lifted word's pitch can't decide it alone.

lessons.text: Passing the next line as context makes a short final word read as a continuation (it rises); dropping the next-line context lets it fall, but with no tag the model may run the words together and lose the beat.

terms: Passing the next line as context can make a short final word read as a continuation

lessons.text: Forcing a fall onto a short word cost the voice clarity: every falling take was rougher and breathier on the word. Measure a word's clarity as the median CPPS over its voiced frames (from 20 ms before the word to 250 ms after Whisper's end), not only by the span's breath index, because H1-H2 follows pitch on a lifted word.

destination.note: A word's clarity is the median CPPS over its voiced frames; a falling take must be at least as clear as the untagged reads (tagloop.emotion, alive_fall).

lessons.text: When a measured target can't be met at full voice, stop generating: give the owner the cleanest alternatives plus the closest rejected take, so they can hear what the target costs. Tagging a line again is a job for the ear, not another generation round.

terms: retagging it is a job for the owner's ear, not another round
Near misses can be added, labelled with what they missed

lessons.text: A one-word pickup (a comp): keep the approved take up to the word, cut inside the silence before it (find the word's audible onset from the audio, since Whisper's word starts run up to 0.3 s early), crossfade 30 ms in the pause, gain the donor so its line's loud part matches, and land the word exactly where the original's did. It costs no credits.

destination.note: `slate voice comp <shot> --word N --from TAKE` (true_onset, splice): no TTS call.

lessons.text: Make prosody rules relative to the voice, never absolute: a voice that always lifts question words can't meet "no rise", not even in its approved takes. The rhetorical rule's target is at least 1 semitone less rise than the voice's untagged takes, and its gate no more than 1 semitone past its most-rising untagged take.

destination.note: The rhetorical intent asks for at least 1 semitone less rise than the untagged reads; the ending gate allows no question word more than 1 semitone past its most-rising untagged read.

terms: on a rhetorical line, no question word rises more than 1 semitone past its untagged reads

lessons.text: A tag can keep full voice and still miss its emotion: "warmly" made one line 1.7 to 3 semitones lower instead of the measured warmth (a lift or a brighter voice), so the line stayed untagged.

terms: The feelings, measured on the emotion span against the untagged reads
destination.note: A tag that keeps full voice but misses its measured feeling isn't picked, and the line stays on its current take.

lessons.text: Pooling more lines' untagged takes changes the pooled calibration a little and can flip a near-edge verdict: re-run every approved and proposed take through the gates after a recalibration.

terms: after a recalibration, re-run every approved and proposed take through the gates

lessons.text: A take that changes length re-times everything after it (shots follow takes: lead, take, tail, hold), so downstream re-timing waits for the owner's approval of the whole track. After it: back up the old takes, swap the approved set in, re-transcribe, rebuild the storyboard, words, shots, timeline, captions and render registry, re-run each act's word and timing checks and event writes and the type check, then the contract stills, the score, the mix and the renders. Check by hand: hand-split number spellings, score landings that drift past the recompose threshold, boundary contracts and frame numbers quoted in docs.

destination.note: `slate make` rebuilds every stale step after a take changes, in order (storyboard, voice, timing, events, render, mix, master, qa); the owner's approval of the whole re-voiced track before re-timing is the VOICE-SWAP gap (L-voice-S019).

terms: Re-time, re-render the affected range and splice it

lessons.text: Before re-timing anything, preview a re-voiced narration as one voice-only track on the storyboard's timeline: each line at -20 LUFS with the cue sheet's fades, each shot grown or shrunk by its take's change, next to the current track made the same way.

terms: -20 LUFS with the cue sheet's fades
destination.note: `slate voice preview`: writes voice/preview/, never a timing file.

terms: The re-voiced narration on the timeline

lessons.text: An approval swap is one command: without its go flag it prints the plan; with it, it uses the exact files the owner heard, records the approval, backs up what it replaces and stops at the first failing step, naming the step and keeping a log.

terms: Raises Refused naming the step that failed
destination.note: `slate voice swap <set> [--go --by NAME]`: without --go the plan (swap.plan).

lessons.text: A "less excited" read is measured against the take the owner called too excited: pitch range (p10-p90, creak removed) at least 1 semitone narrower, peak lift at least 1 semitone lower, less rise on the key word, an energy swing no larger, and not rushed (at most 5% over the fastest untagged rate). A guard keeps it from going flat: range at least 75% of the untagged median, median pitch no more than 1.5 semitones under, no more than 10% slower.

destination.note: The calmer intent, against the take the owner called too excited, with its not-flat guard.

lessons.text: Many takes drop an octave into creak for the last 20 to 50 ms of a word: measure a final word's rise on its voiced, creak-free frames, or the drop reads as a fall.
When a measure's rule has to change during a round, write the change down before the pick, and keep the earlier gates unchanged beside it.

terms: each written down before the pick

lessons.text: Measure where a voice's harshness lives before polishing it: the long-term average spectrum in third-octave bands on speech frames at -20 LUFS, against the ANSI S3.5 standard speech spectrum set equal over 500 Hz-1 kHz; band levels for the lows, the body, the 1-5 kHz clarity band, the 2-5 kHz edge, 5-9 kHz sibilance and the air; and the hottest edge and sibilance moments, word by word.

destination.note: `slate voice analyze --spectrum`: the third-octave long-term spectrum over speech at -20 LUFS against ANSI S3.5 (set equal over 500 Hz-1 kHz), the band levels, the edge and sibilance over time, the hottest words (ringed on the A/B sheet) and spectrum.png; the polish trial pools every line into the same chart and writes a harshest-moments reel (each moment unpolished, then at every strength). Closed 2026-10-01.

lessons.text: A generated voice's harshness can sit at the very top, not in 2-5 kHz: one voice climbed 12 dB from 5 to 10 kHz where speech keeps falling, carried a glassy comb of harmonics on its vowels and peaked its sibilance at 10-11 kHz, while its 2-5 kHz sat 3 to 7 dB under natural speech. A static 2-5 kHz cut would only dull it and cost the mix's clarity: measure first.

terms: measure where a voice's harshness lives before tuning its chain
A static cut at 2-5 kHz would only have dulled

lessons.text: The studio vocal chain, in order: a 12 dB/octave high-pass (70-80 Hz); a gentle, wide cut where the take measures boxy or honky; moderate compression on the take brought to -20 LUFS (2 to 3:1, a few dB on loud syllables); a dynamic cut on 2-5 kHz only while a consonant dominates that band; a split-band de-esser (a zero-phase band and its exact complement) cutting only while sibilance dominates the whole sound, with a few ms of look-ahead; a touch of presence; a warmth low shelf and a high shelf easing a glassy top; a small, short, band-limited synthetic room 18 to 21 dB under the dry voice; then loudness back to the take's own integrated loudness, true peak at or under -1 dBTP.

destination.note: The chain in the films' order; the films' tuning carries over unchanged (tests/voice/test_voice_polish_parity.py).

terms: a dynamic cut on 2-5 kHz, only while a consonant dominates the band

lessons.text: Every polish stage keeps the take's length sample for sample, so no shot, word or cue moves, and every take is worked at -20 LUFS so each threshold means the same on every line.

Tune the chain per voice from its own measurements (one voice's harshness was a glassy top and 10-11 kHz sibilance; another's was 5-8 kHz sibilance, a presence bump and boxy low mids, with no glassy top) and offer strengths that bracket the owner's middle, a subtler and a warmer side, rather than one setting.

destination.note: A voice's tuning lives in its profile (`polish`), with named strengths that bracket the owner's middle (A subtler, B warmer).

lessons.text: A strength between "barely noticeable" and "clearly warmer" measured as: sibilance peaks down about 6 and 9 dB, the glassy top 5.5 and 8 dB, only 0.7 and 1.4 dB of 1-5 kHz removed, an overall spectral change of 2.5 to 3.7 dB, and pitch, timing and formants unchanged.

Report what the polish did, per line and pooled, on the delivered files at equal loudness: sibilance peaks (the loudest 5 ms of 5.5-12.5 kHz), the glassy top on voiced frames, 2-5 kHz, the 1-5 kHz energy removed (the band the mix's clarity rule checks), warmth (80-500 Hz against 1-5 kHz), the compressor's gain reduction and the overall spectral change; with an LTAS chart against natural speech, every line's spectrogram with its hottest moments ringed, and a harshest-moments reel (each moment unpolished, then each strength).

destination.note: Per line and pooled (summarize_pairs): sibilance and edge peaks, 1-5 kHz removed, warmth, the compressor's gain reduction and the overall spectral change, at equal loudness; the LTAS chart, ringed moments and the harshest-moments reel are the VOICE-SPECTRUM gap (L-voice-S024).

lessons.text: Keep the unpolished clean takes as the measurement source: the polish is the last step on the film-stage take, a polished baseline would make new takes look harsh against the voice, and re-pacing from the clean take needs the polish again.

destination.note: Timing resolves a shot's take in the voice module's own order (polished, paced, clean, raw), so the cue sheets and the mix play the polished take, while breath, pitch and tag measures still read the take before its polish (VoiceFilm.unpolished_audio). Closed 2026-10-01; `slate demo` fails if the cue sheet or the mix doesn't play the polished takes.

also.note: The breath and tag measures read the take before its polish (tests/voice/test_voice_quality_gates.py::test_polished_takes_are_measured_on_their_unpolished_source).

lessons.text: Listening files compare at equal loudness (each line at -20 LUFS) so nothing wins on level, in a stated order, each with the decision it asks for ("Tell me A, B or C").

destination.note: Every listening reel is level-matched to -20 LUFS, in a stated order with its listing; the ABC reel puts the film's current take first.

lessons.text: Polishing the narration changes the mix: it gave up about 0.8 dB of 1-5 kHz, so the mix's clarity guard had to re-solve its accent rides (with the old rides frozen one word fell to 8.3 dB clear). A polish on approved narration means re-solving the mix's rides; a span pinned to approved rides can't keep them.

terms: A voice change moves the balance
a span pinned to rides approved before the polish can't keep them
A polish moves the mix too

lessons.text: Test a voice change on the clip the owner knows best, with every mix setting pinned to that clip's approved build, and prove the pin first by rebuilding the approved mix sample for sample before changing only the voice.

terms: on the clip the owner knows best
rebuilding the approved mix sample for sample

lessons.text: The polish needs nothing paid or downloaded: a local audio-plugin host library gave the EQ and the compressor, and numpy and scipy the dynamic bands and the room.

Ask the owner for the target in their own terms before tuning (where the harshness is, the reference sound such as "a podcast host, a little room, warm and present", and how strong a change), then bracket their middle with two strengths.
